verses.verse:
प्राणस्य सोधयेन्मांर्गम् पूरक कुम्भक रेचकैः।
टकावुच्यार्य जिह्वांश्च व्यायामेनांगुलीयकान्।६२।
verses.text: One should purify the path of the breath by pūraka, kumbhaka and recaka (inhalation, retention and exhalation); the tongue by pronouncing ṭa and ka; and the fingers by exercise.

commentary.text: That is, one should perfect the prāṇa (breath) by prāṇāyāma (breath control), the tongue by ṭa and ka, and the fingers by vyāyāma (exercise).

following.text: Sādhanā of the Prāṇa (Practice of the Breath)

Broadly, for the sādhanā (practice) of the breath other ācāryas have taught this procedure: pūraka (drawing [the breath] up), kumbhaka (holding the breath) and recaka (letting the breath out slowly). But for bānsurī players this procedure is mastered effortlessly anyway. So one should especially practise bhastrikā prāṇāyāma, that is (moving the breath up and down at a fast pace for 2 minutes), so that a sweet kampana (vibration) arises in the nāda (sound). As when, after a gong is struck, a beautiful wave-like vibrating sound is heard for a while, that is called uttama (excellent) vibration. As a lamp's flame wavers in a light breeze, so an adhama (poor) vibration lives naturally, as a fault, in the notes of all sādhakas (practitioners); this vibration is wholly to be given up. And regular vibration is wholly to be taken up. This procedure is like levelling the natural unevenness of barren land and making a regular rise and fall in the form of beautiful garden beds. Only then will the plants of the notes look beautiful in that bed. Do this procedure daily in the early morning in the winter days, increasing it from 2 minutes to 5 minutes. Then if you make the sound vibrate regularly on any one note of the bānsurī, a single note will keep the mind immersed in bliss.

It is proven by experience that touching the jihvā (tongue) in turn to the throat, the palate, the roof of the mouth and the teeth produces the sounds (ka), (ca), (ṭa) and (ta). In the same way, keep blowing into the bānsurī while saying ṭa and ka quickly and without a break, many times over. Just as the dir dir of the sitar turns one note into equal pieces, so [this] will make the sound coming out of the bānsurī beautiful with equal strokes. If at first some fault is heard in the breath because of this action, do not be put off by it; keep practising for a long time, with confidence, like this: (ṭa ka ṭa ka ṭa ka). Once it is mastered, it will become beautiful. These same two syllables will turn Sa into Sa Sa Sa Sa and Re into Re Re Re Re.
If, instead of ṭa-ka, one relies on some other syllable such as ca or ta, the practitioner will regret it later, because along with the breath the saliva must also be kept in check.

It is true that the fingers gain strength from repeatedly and quickly gripping something and letting it go; this natural exercise goes on anyway in various tasks such as washing clothes. But because in these tasks there is no devotion to the exercise, or absorption in it, we do not give it the place of sādhanā (practice). So, with the fingers held straight on a table and without moving the hand, keep striking with just one finger, with full strength, a hundred times in a row, counting; then strike with the second, third and fourth finger in the same way. Then close the holes on the bānsurī and, in the same way, keep striking each finger quickly on the hole of the bānsurī until pain arises at the root of the finger. Then strike two fingers together, and then three fingers together. By doing this every day without a break, the speed of the fingers will keep increasing month by month, and this will give you good help in the svara practice that comes later. Then, if you also want to learn another instrument, such as the tabla, you will progress quickly in that too. The following śloka points to these very things.
